description.text:
The first numbered Japanese promos: 47 cards, 001/P to 047/P, released from July 2001 to July 2002. They were the first Japanese promos to carry the black star PROMO symbol of the English promos, with a P after the number in place of a set total, which every numbered Japanese promo set since has followed, usually with a new suffix for each series.

They came with the film Celebi: A Timeless Encounter and its video release, with CoroCoro Comic and Pokémon Card Trainers magazine, in All Nippon Airways' summer 2001 campaign, the Starter Triple Get Campaign and two McDonald's promotions in 2002, at the Pokémon Centers in Tokyo and Osaka for the opening of the New York Pokémon Center, and at events: Tropical Wind for the players in the 2001 Tropical Mega Battle finals, the Crystal, Boost and Warp Energy of Battle Road Summer 2002, and six cards from the Pokémon Happy Adventure Rally 2002.

description.text:
Given by All Nippon Airways in its Pokémon Card e ANA Special '01 Version campaign. Passengers who flew two one-way ANA domestic flights between 13 July and 30 September 2001 pasted the two ticket stubs on an application postcard, and everyone who applied was mailed this card and Larvitar 005/P as a set, from early September. ANA had given away seven Pokémon cards of its own design since its Pokémon Jets began flying in June 1998, and its press release introduced Pokémon Card e, the new cards a Game Boy Advance could read through a card reader, due out that autumn.

Hironobu Yoshida drew the pair as a game of hide-and-seek: each card shows the other Pokémon hiding behind a hedge, and scanning both cards' dot-code strips with the e-Reader starts a hide-and-seek game. That summer ANA also showed the short film Pikachu's Exciting Hide-and-Seek on its flights.

description.text: Given with Pokémon Card Trainers Vol. 13, the September 2001 issue of the Pokémon Card Fan Club's members-only magazine, together with Bill 009/P. Hajime Kusajima drew it.

The card of the 2001 International Tropical Mega Battle, held at the Hilton Hawaiian Village in Honolulu on 25 and 26 August 2001 for 23 players aged 14 or under from 10 countries. For its VS Shield Battle every player was given the same 30-card deck, the Tyranitar half deck sold in Japan from 7 July 2001, with this card in place of its Tyranitar and Darkness Energy. The Japanese players' decks held this numbered card. Players from other countries got the deck in their own language, or in English, with an unnumbered Tropical Breeze; the French and Italian ones have never been seen.

In Japanese the card is Tropical Wind, the name and effect of the 1999 Tropical Mega Battle's card, and Sumiyoshi Kizuki drew both, but this picture is new, with Psyduck again lying in a hammock with a ukulele. Played, it makes you flip a coin: on heads each player removes up to two damage counters from their Active Pokémon, on tails both Active Pokémon fall Asleep.

Given with Pokémon Card Trainers Vol. 13, the September 2001 issue of the Pokémon Card Fan Club's members-only magazine, together with Celebi 007/P. Ken Sugimori's Bill, called Masaki in Japan, stands in front of a brick wall; he is a Supporter who lets you draw two cards.

Given with the December 2001 issue of CoroCoro Comic, out in November 2001. Mitsuhiro Arita's Ho-Oh spreads its wings in front of a rainbow.

CoroCoro's next issue gave Arita's Rapidash, 011/P. Wizards of the Coast printed the same art in English as Black Star promo 52, which came with Rapidash 51 in the November 2002 issue of Nintendo Power.

description.text:
A prize of the Starter Triple Get Campaign, which ran from 1 December 2001 to 30 April 2002 tied to the e-Card starter deck. Each deck held a postcard: players stuck on the proofs of purchase of three starter decks, picked one of two courses, and mailed it in. This card is in the Red/Green course with Blastoise 013/P and Charizard 014/P, and each winner got all three, in a Pokémon card game envelope with a winning notice. After each of five monthly deadlines 1,000 winners were drawn for each course, 5,000 per course in all by Pokumon's count, so 5,000 copies of each card were given out.

The six cards, the last evolutions of the Kanto and Johto starter Pokémon, are holofoil versions of cards that the main set printed without holofoil. Atsuko Nishida drew this one.

description.text:
Given to members who joined or renewed the Pokémon Card Fan Club in 2002, with a zippered card holder printed "Pokemon Card Fan Club". The club began in 1999 with its magazine, Trainers, and ended in December 2002, when the Pokémon Players Club replaced it.

Imakuni?, the singer who appears on many of the game's joke cards, is on the picture. The text, in handwriting, has each player turn all their Prize cards face up and then turn their deck face up too: "Don't be shy." A red line says it can't be used in official tournaments.

description.text:
The numbered print of the card of the New Kangaskhan Rule, a two-player tag-team side event at Japan's Battle Road Spring and Summer 2002 tournaments. Each team built two decks, one of old-back cards and one of current-back cards. When this card is played, every player shuffles their hand back into its own deck, and their partner may draw up to 5 cards and take over. Its red line reads 新ガルーラルール専用カード, a card only for New Kangaskhan Rule games. Tomokazu Komiya drew it.

Each player got two copies at the side event. Readers of Trainers magazine Vol. 17 could also trade a voucher from page 21 for two copies at the summer events, or claim them by mail afterwards. The card was also printed without a number, and the pages that show both don't say which print went where.

description.text:
Given at Pokémon Festa 2002, a touring summer event where visitors played the Pokémon video games and the card game and watched the films, held from 20 July to 11 August 2002 and sharing five of its venues with the Battle Road Summer 2002 tournaments. Visitors who collected at least three stamps by taking part in different events at a venue got this card as an orienteering prize.

Midori Harada drew Pikachu twice in this scene, with Mewtwo behind: the other is Pikachu 044/P, one of the six cards of the Pokémon Happy Adventure Rally 2002. Both have the attack Smash Link, which spares Pikachu its recoil damage if Mewtwo is on your Bench.

description.text:
One of three holofoil special Energy cards that players at Battle Road Summer 2002 could get for points earned in the side events, with Boost Energy 040/P and Warp Energy 041/P; the points also bought card sleeves or Imakuni?'s signature. Battle Road Summer 2002 was Japan's summer tournament circuit, held at seven venues on nine days from Sapporo on 20 July to Fukuoka on 11 August 2002, five of them at Pokémon Festa 2002.

Kai Ishikawa drew all three. It counts as one Energy of every type of the basic Energy cards on the Pokémon it is attached to.

One of three holofoil special Energy cards that players at Battle Road Summer 2002 could get for points earned in the side events, with Crystal Energy 039/P and Warp Energy 041/P; the points also bought card sleeves or Imakuni?'s signature. Battle Road Summer 2002 was Japan's summer tournament circuit, held at seven venues on nine days from Sapporo on 20 July to Fukuoka on 11 August 2002, five of them at Pokémon Festa 2002.

Kai Ishikawa drew all three. It can be attached only to an evolved Pokémon, provides three Colorless Energy, keeps that Pokémon from retreating, and is discarded at the end of the turn.

One of three holofoil special Energy cards that players at Battle Road Summer 2002 could get for points earned in the side events, with Crystal Energy 039/P and Boost Energy 040/P; the points also bought card sleeves or Imakuni?'s signature. Battle Road Summer 2002 was Japan's summer tournament circuit, held at seven venues on nine days from Sapporo on 20 July to Fukuoka on 11 August 2002, five of them at Pokémon Festa 2002.

Kai Ishikawa drew all three. It provides one Colorless Energy, and when you attach it from your hand to your Active Pokémon, that Pokémon switches with one of your Benched Pokémon.

One of the six cards of the Pokémon Happy Adventure Rally 2002, JR East's Pokémon rally that year: participants collected six Pokémon Card e cards at stations of Tokyo's Yamanote Line and at Pokémon Center Tokyo, and found the goal station from hints left at special points. JR East has run Pokémon rallies at Tokyo stations since 1997.

Midori Harada drew all six, Celebi with Entei 043/P, Pikachu 044/P, Pichu 045/P, Mewtwo 046/P and Lugia 047/P, and their pictures join into one scene. Each has an attack or Poké-Power whose name contains "Link". Celebi's is Para Link.

One of the six cards of the Pokémon Happy Adventure Rally 2002, JR East's Pokémon rally that year: participants collected six Pokémon Card e cards at stations of Tokyo's Yamanote Line and at Pokémon Center Tokyo, and found the goal station from hints left at special points. JR East has run Pokémon rallies at Tokyo stations since 1997.

Midori Harada drew all six, Pichu with Celebi 042/P, Entei 043/P, Pikachu 044/P, Mewtwo 046/P and Lugia 047/P, and their pictures join into one scene. Each has an attack or Poké-Power whose name contains "Link". Pichu's is Heal Link.
